title: PROVERBS DOESN’T ONLY SAY “DON’T COMMIT ADULTERY”—It Tells a Man What to Enjoy Instead
paragraphs: PROVERBS DOESN’T ONLY SAY “DON’T COMMIT ADULTERY”—It Tells a Man What to Enjoy Instead
Proverbs 5 contains a message about lust, marriage, desire, and faithfulness that many men desperately need to hear.
There is a kind of faithfulness that is technically obedient but emotionally starving.
A man can say, “I have never slept with another woman,” and still spend years feeding his imagination with women who are not his wife.
He can avoid the hotel room and still live inside the fantasy.
He can never touch another woman and still secretly compare his wife to bodies on a screen.
He can sit beside her in church, sing about holiness, come home with her, sleep beside her...
and slowly train his heart to desire everybody except the woman he promised God he would love.
Then Proverbs 5 walks into that hidden room.
And what it says is far more confronting—and far more beautiful—than simply:
“Don’t commit adultery.”
Because God does not merely tell a husband what he must run from.
He tells him where his desire should run toward.
That difference changes everything.
Proverbs 5 begins like a father grabbing his son by the shoulders before the young man destroys something he will spend years wishing he could recover.
“Pay attention.”
“Listen.”
“Keep discretion.”
“Guard your lips.”
Then comes the warning.
Forbidden desire rarely introduces itself as destruction.
It arrives sweet.
The forbidden woman’s lips “drip honey.”
Her speech is smoother than oil.
That is the terrifying intelligence of temptation.
Sin usually does not show you the ending when it introduces you to the beginning.
Pornography does not show you the marriage becoming colder.
The flirtation does not show you your wife crying.
The private messages do not show you your children asking what happened.
The fantasy does not show you how comparison can slowly make a real spouse seem ordinary beside an endless digital parade of edited bodies.
The affair does not introduce itself by saying:
“Hello. I am here to fracture trust, wound your family, poison your conscience, steal your peace, and leave memories you cannot erase.”
No.
It tastes like honey first.
Proverbs says the end becomes bitter.
That is why Scripture is not prudish about sexual desire.
Scripture is protective of it.
There is a difference.
God did not invent sexuality and then become embarrassed by His own creation.
Before pornography existed, before adultery existed, before lust distorted desire, before shame entered human experience, God created man and woman and called His creation very good.
Sexual desire is not the enemy.
Disordered desire is.
Desire detached from covenant is.
Desire trained to consume instead of cherish is.
Desire that turns another human being into an object is.
And this is where Proverbs 5 becomes startling.
After warning the son about forbidden sexuality, the father does not tell him to become emotionally numb.
He does not say, “Stop desiring.”
He redirects the desire.
Listen to Proverbs 5:18 in Hebrew:
יְהִי־מְקוֹרְךָ בָרוּךְ וּשְׂמַח מֵאֵשֶׁת נְעוּרֶךָ
Yehi-meqorkha barukh, u-semach me’eshet ne‘urekha.
A faithful rendering is:
“Let your fountain be blessed, and rejoice in the wife of your youth.”
Notice that word:
וּשְׂמַח — u-semach.
Rejoice.
Not merely tolerate.
Not merely remain legally married to.
Not merely resist everybody else while quietly resenting her.
Rejoice.
Enjoy the covenant God has given you.
Delight in your wife.
See her again.
That is what many discussions about purity miss.
Biblical sexual holiness is not merely the absence of adultery.
It includes the cultivation of covenant affection.
Proverbs continues with language so intimate that nobody can honestly accuse the Bible of treating marital sexuality as dirty.
The Hebrew of Proverbs 5:19 says:
אַיֶּלֶת אֲהָבִים וְיַעֲלַת־חֵן דַּדֶּיהָ יְרַוֻּךָ בְכָל־עֵת בְּאַהֲבָתָהּ תִּשְׁגֶּה תָמִיד
The imagery describes the wife as lovely and graceful and tells the husband to find continuing satisfaction in her body and to be continually captivated by her love.
Read that again.
Captivated by her love.
God’s answer to forbidden desire is not merely:
“No.”
There is also a holy:
“Here.”
Here is covenant.
Here is faithfulness.
Here is intimacy without hiding.
Here is a woman you do not have to delete from your messages when someone enters the room.
Here is love that can survive morning light.
Here is desire that does not require betrayal.
Here is pleasure that does not need another person’s devastation to exist.
Here is the wife of your youth.
Rejoice in her.
And perhaps that hurts to read.
Because maybe something happened along the way.
Life happened.
Children came.
Bills came.
Arguments came.
Bodies changed.
Schedules became crowded.
Exhaustion replaced anticipation.
You stopped dating each other.
You stopped talking deeply.
You stopped touching without wanting something.
You stopped noticing.
And somewhere in the slow erosion of ordinary life, temptation discovered the distance.
Maybe nobody knows.
Maybe your wife does not know what appears on your phone when she is asleep.
Maybe your husband does not know who you think about.
Maybe you tell yourself it is harmless because nothing physical happened.
Maybe you have learned how to clear history better than you have learned how to confess sin.
Maybe there is a name you would never want your spouse to see.
Maybe there is an account you would panic to have opened in church.
Maybe your body has remained in the marriage while your imagination has been wandering outside it for years.
Proverbs does not allow us to call that freedom.
It asks a devastating question:
Why become intoxicated with forbidden love when covenant love has been placed before you?
And then Proverbs 5 pulls back the curtain even farther.
It reminds us that our lives are lived before God.
A man may erase his browser history.
He cannot erase anything from the sight of God.
A woman may hide the conversation.
God already saw it.
You can fool a spouse.
You can fool a pastor.
You can fool your friends.
You can sometimes fool yourself.
But you cannot hide your paths from the Lord.
That sounds terrifying.
And if Proverbs were the end of the Bible, terror might be where we would have to stop.
But Proverbs is not the end of the story.
Jesus Christ came.
And suddenly the man hiding in sexual sin is not merely standing before a warning.
He is standing before a Savior.
This matters because some people reading this article have already crossed the line Proverbs warned them not to cross.
You did not merely look.
You went.
You did not merely fantasize.
You touched.
You lied.
You betrayed.
Maybe the affair ended years ago, but sometimes you still hear the wreckage inside your conscience.
Maybe pornography has owned a hidden room in your life for so long that you cannot remember who you were before it.
Maybe your marriage bears scars created by your own decisions.
Maybe you are reading Proverbs 5 thinking:
“This is what I should have heard before I destroyed everything.”
But hear the Gospel.
Jesus did not come only for people who obeyed Proverbs 5 perfectly.
Jesus came for sinners.
That does not make adultery small.
Grace never needs to make sin smaller in order to make Christ bigger.
At the cross, we discover precisely how serious sin is—and how astonishing the mercy of God is.
Jesus speaks about adultery at the level of the heart. He refuses to let outward respectability become a hiding place for inward lust.
But the same Jesus who exposes sin receives repentant sinners.
The Gospel does not say, “Pretend it never happened.”
The Gospel says, “Bring what happened into the light.”
Repentance is not learning to hide more religiously.
It is agreeing with God about your sin and turning toward Him.
And grace is not permission to keep returning to darkness.
Grace teaches us that we no longer have to live there.
That means the husband trapped in pornography is not being called merely to feel ashamed.
He is being called home.
The wife emotionally attached to another man is not being invited to invent better excuses.
She is being called home.
The spouse who has committed adultery is not promised freedom from every earthly consequence, nor is wounded trust repaired by a few emotional words.
But in Christ, genuine repentance, forgiveness before God, transformed living, accountability, truth, and restoration are real possibilities.
Sometimes rebuilding human trust takes a long time.
Sometimes consequences remain.
Grace is not amnesia.
Forgiveness does not magically make every wound disappear.
But failure does not possess greater saving power than the blood of Jesus.
That is the scandal of grace.
The cross takes people whose stories contain chapters they would burn if they could...
and Christ begins writing something new.
Not because adultery was acceptable.
Not because lust was harmless.
Not because betrayal did not matter.
But because Jesus is greater than the worst chapter of a genuinely repentant sinner’s story.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
And for those who are married, repentance may become painfully practical.
Look at your spouse again.
Not as the person who competes unsuccessfully with your fantasies.
As the person you covenanted to love.
Stop feeding desires that make covenant intimacy taste ordinary.
You cannot endlessly consume fantasy and then wonder why reality seems less stimulating.
Fantasy is designed around you.
Marriage requires you to love someone other than yourself.
Pornography asks nothing from you except consumption.
Covenant asks for patience.
Sacrifice.
Communication.
Forgiveness.
Tenderness.
Self-control.
Presence.
Faithfulness.
And that is precisely why covenant can become something pornography can never become:
love.
Your spouse is not content.
Your spouse is a person bearing the image of God.
And Proverbs does not tell you to use that person.
It calls you into covenant delight.
Maybe you need to remember the person you married before resentment buried the memory.
Remember her laugh.
Remember his nervousness.
Remember those conversations that somehow lasted until morning.
Remember when you prayed for the person you now sometimes take for granted.
Remember when holding that hand felt like an answered prayer.
Bodies age.
Hair changes.
Skin changes.
Strength changes.
Hormones change.
Pregnancy changes bodies.
Sickness changes bodies.
Time changes every photograph eventually.
But covenant love has the opportunity to become something lust can never become:
deeper.
There is something profoundly beautiful about being able to look at someone decades later and know:
I chose you when we were young.
I chose you when life was easy.
I chose you when life hurt.
I chose you when we misunderstood each other.
I chose you when your body changed.
I chose you when mine did too.
I chose you when temptation whispered.
And by the grace of God...
I am still choosing you.
That is not boring Christianity.
That is warfare.
That is worship expressed through faithfulness.
That is a quiet rebellion against a culture constantly teaching people that dissatisfaction deserves disobedience.
And if your marriage is hurting, Proverbs 5 should never be weaponized to demand sexual access, excuse coercion, silence abuse, or pretend serious relational wounds do not exist.
Biblical intimacy belongs inside covenant love, mutual honor, faithfulness, and care.
Some marriages need difficult conversations.
Some need pastoral help.
Some need qualified counseling.
Some situations involving abuse require safety, wise intervention, and appropriate authorities.
“Rejoice in the wife of your youth” is not permission to dominate another human being.
It is a summons away from exploitation and toward faithful covenant love.
And perhaps you are single.
Proverbs 5 still speaks to you.
The habits you cultivate before marriage do not magically disappear at a wedding.
A wedding ring cannot crucify lust.
Only surrender to Christ begins transforming the heart.
Do not spend your single years training your mind to consume hundreds or thousands of bodies and assume that one day you will effortlessly become satisfied with one covenant partner.
Learn now that another human being was never created to be consumed.
Learn now to look at people as image-bearers rather than products.
Learn now to flee what feeds darkness.
Learn now to confess.
Learn now to pray.
Learn now to bring secret things into the light.
And if you fall, do not make peace with the fall.
Run to Christ.
Again.
Not casually.
Not presumptuously.
Repentantly.
Honestly.
Completely.
Maybe this article exposed something you have kept hidden.
Sit with it.
What is God putting His finger on?
A screen?
A conversation?
A fantasy?
An affair?
A resentment?
A marriage you have stopped nurturing?
A secret you need to confess?
A spouse you need to begin cherishing again?
A heart that has learned to hunger for forbidden water while neglecting its own well?
Be honest.
This may have hit harder than you expected.
If your marriage has survived a season you thought would destroy it, your testimony might become someone else’s reason not to quit.
And if someone came to your mind while reading this, do not use this article as a weapon against them.
Send it with love.
Share it with the young man who needs to understand purity before temptation writes consequences into his future.
Share it with the woman who needs to remember that conviction is not the same thing as condemnation for those who turn to Christ.
Not because an article can keep you faithful.
It cannot.
But there may come a night when temptation begins negotiating with you again, and you need to remember what it refused to tell you:
Honey can become bitter.
Secret pleasure can become public grief.
And God has called His people to something better than constantly asking how close they can stand to destruction without falling in.
Invite your family.
Invite your friends.
Invite struggling believers.
Invite the Christian who has grown lukewarm.
Invite the seeker.
Even invite the unbelieving friend who has questions about whether Christianity has anything meaningful to say about desire, failure, shame, forgiveness, and becoming new.
That support should never be given because you were pressured into believing that paying Gospel Warrior is required for God to accept you or bless you.
The Gospel cannot be purchased.
Scripture teaches believers to give willingly rather than under compulsion, while also recognizing the legitimacy of materially supporting Gospel ministry.
Come to Jesus.
Because Proverbs 5 ultimately forces every one of us to confront a deeper question than whether somebody caught us.
What has captured our heart?
Forbidden desire promises intoxication.
Christ offers transformation.
Sin says, “Hide.”
Jesus says, “Come into the light.”
Shame says, “Your worst chapter is your identity.”
The cross says, “Repent, come to Me, and receive mercy.”
And perhaps tonight, somewhere behind a locked door, a man will finally delete what has been poisoning his marriage.
Perhaps a woman will end the conversation she knows has crossed a boundary.
Perhaps a husband will put down his phone and actually look at his wife.
Perhaps a wife will reach again for the hand she stopped reaching for.
Perhaps someone who committed adultery years ago will finally stop running from God and discover that repentance still has a road home.
Perhaps a young person will decide before marriage that pornography will not disciple their sexuality.
Perhaps somebody reading these words will whisper through tears:
“Jesus... I need You to rewrite this.”
And He is exactly the Savior sinners need.
Not a Savior for imaginary people with spotless histories.
A Savior for the guilty.
A Savior for the ashamed.
A Savior for adulterers who repent.
A Savior for the lustful who surrender.
A Savior for wounded spouses.
A Savior for broken marriages.
A Savior for people whose private histories make them wonder whether holiness could ever become beautiful again.
Proverbs warns us because God loves us too much to call destruction freedom.
Christ receives repentant sinners because mercy is not something we achieve.
It is something He purchased.
So do not merely spend your life trying not to drink from the wrong well.
Ask Christ to teach your heart to love what is good.
To treasure covenant.
To honor bodies rather than consume them.
To rejoice without hiding.
To desire without betraying.
To become faithful when nobody is watching.
And when temptation offers you honey, remember where the road ends.
Then remember something even greater:
Jesus does not merely call you away from the darkness you desired—He can transform the heart that desired it.
Because maybe the most beautiful testimony is not, “I was never tempted.”
Maybe it is:
“The thing that almost destroyed my story did not get to write the ending—Jesus did.”
